The laws in these chapters were about food, having babies and skin diseases. They were also about mould and liquid waste from people’s bodies.

There were two main points with these laws in Leviticus. The first was that the Israelites were to be different from other people groups. The foods they were allowed to eat and those they weren’t allowed to eat showed this. Being different showed that the Israelites didn’t follow the false gods of other people groups. They followed the true God who was holy.

The second main point was that God is the God of life. Death is the result of sin. God doesn’t want sin and death to be in the world that he created. So things that had to do with death made people unclean. God’s people received rules from him about how to be considered clean and pure. Being clean and pure allowed them to worship God together with the community.

These chapters explain the rules about purity. Mixing different types of animals was forbidden (see {{Deuteronomy 22:9-11|Deuteronomy 22:9–11}}). This is because it opposed God's natural order. Creatures like fish without fins and scales, meat-eating animals, crawling insects, and animals without split hooves were considered "abnormal." They crossed the boundaries between "normal" types and were not suitable for food or offerings (see also {{Deuteronomy 14:1-21|Deuteronomy 14:1–21}}). The dietary laws intended to set Israel apart as a holy people from other nations ({{Leviticus 11:44-45|Leviticus 11:44–45}}).
*these ones you may eat:* The Israelites considered animals with split hooves that chew cud to be "normal" and ceremonially clean (see also {{Deuteronomy 14:3-21|Deuteronomy 14:3–21}}).

Some scholars think people avoided ceremonially unclean animals for health reasons. But evidence does not support this suggestion. Horse meat, for instance, is as healthy as beef, yet it was "unclean" because the horse does not have a split hoof (see {{Leviticus 11:2-3|Leviticus 11:2–3}}). These rules existed because an unclean animal was not suitable as an offering to God. So, it was likewise not suitable as food for God's people. 

Jesus proclaimed all foods clean for Christians ({{Mark 7:14-19|Mark 7:14–19}}). This teaching was confirmed in Peter’s vision ({{Acts 10:9-16|Acts 10:9–16}}).
The rock badger and the rabbit do not actually chew cud, even though it looks like they do. They are ceremonially unclean because they lack split hooves.
*the creatures that live in the water:* The Israelites considered animals from the water to be clean (acceptable for food and for ritual use) only if they had both fins and scales
The prohibition included fish like eels and sharks, which have fins but no scales. It also included crustaceans and mollusks, which have neither fins nor scales.

The list of ceremonially unclean birds includes birds of prey and scavengers. These birds often touch dead animals and blood, making them unclean and unfit for eating and offerings. Bats fly but are not birds ({{Leviticus 11:19|Leviticus 11:19}}). So, they are "abnormal" and ceremonially unclean.

*insects that walk on all fours: those having jointed legs above their feet:* This phrase excludes creatures that creep or crawl close to the ground ({{Leviticus 11:27|Leviticus 11:27}}). {{Leviticus 11:42|Leviticus 11:42}} says that creatures with many legs, like centipedes, are ceremonially unclean. Locusts and grasshoppers are examples of ceremonially clean insects (see {{Matthew 3:4|Matthew 3:4}}).
*unclean until evening:* Anyone who touched a ceremonially unclean animal that was dead would be unclean until evening. In Israel, evening marked the start of the next day.

This list of ceremonially unclean creatures that crawl includes both warm-blooded and cold-blooded animals that move along the ground. Snakes are also part of this group ({{Leviticus 11:42|Leviticus 11:42}}).

Dead animals could make objects and people ceremonially unclean. Even a ceremonially clean animal that died without its blood drained was unclean ({{Leviticus 11:39-40|Leviticus 11:39–40}}). If a person touched the body of a dead animal, they were unclean until evening. Household items that touched the body of a dead animal needed purification or the people had to destroy the items ({{Leviticus 11:25|11:25}}, {{Leviticus 11:28|28}}, {{Leviticus 11:32|32}}, {{Leviticus 11:40|40}}; {{Leviticus 11:33|11:33}}, {{Leviticus 11:35|35}}).
A cistern was a hole dug into the ground or rock. They often lined it with plaster to hold rain and surface water.

People probably moistened grain with water to cook it for food. Eating contaminated grain was like eating a dead animal. But if they planted the grain, the new plant and its grain were ceremonially clean.

Israelites could not consume blood ({{Leviticus 7:26|Leviticus 7:26}}). They could eat an animal only after draining and properly disposing of the blood ({{Leviticus 17:13|17:13}}). If a ceremonially clean animal died naturally and did not have its blood drained, it became ceremonially unclean. An Israelite could give or sell such an animal to foreigners but could not eat it ({{Deuteronomy 14:21|Deuteronomy 14:21}}).

- *I am the LORD your God:* See study note on Leviticus 18:2. 

- *be holy, because I am holy:* These words express the main theme of Leviticus: God is holy. They must consider and treat God as holy. God expects holiness from his people ({{Leviticus 10:3|Leviticus 10:3}}; {{Leviticus 19:2|19:2}}). This verse teaches that God's character influences those who make a covenant with him (see also {{Leviticus 11:45|11:45}}; {{Leviticus 20:7|20:7}}, {{Leviticus 20:26|26}}; {{Leviticus 21:8|21:8}}, {{Leviticus 21:15|15}}; {{Leviticus 22:9|22:9}}, {{Leviticus 22:16|16}}, {{Leviticus 22:32|32}}). They must become holy in their actions ({{Exodus 22:31|Exodus 22:31}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:9|Deuteronomy 28:9}}; compare {{1 Peter 1:16|1 Peter 1:16}}).

*brought you up out of the land of Egypt: *This phrase or a similar one appears often in the first five books of the Bible (see {{Leviticus 19:36|Leviticus 19:36}}; {{Leviticus 22:33|22:33}}; {{Leviticus 25:38|25:38}}; {{Leviticus 26:13|26:13}}; {{Exodus 13:9|Exodus 13:9}}; {{Exodus 20:2|20:2}}; {{Numbers 15:41|Numbers 15:41}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:37|Deuteronomy 4:37}}). Each time, it reminds the Israelites, God's chosen people, of God's great act of freeing them from Egypt. Other verses in the Old Testament often mention the exodus event ({{Psalm 80:8|Psalms 80:8}}; {{Psalm 106:21|106:21}}; {{Isaiah 11:16|Isaiah 11:16}}; {{Jeremiah 34:13|Jeremiah 34:13}}; {{Hosea 12:9|Hosea 12:9}}; {{Hosea 13:4|13:4}}; {{Amos 2:10|Amos 2:10}}).

These verses explain the rules about childbirth. Any bodily discharge, including blood, was "abnormal" because it weakened the person and made them ceremonially unclean (see study notes on Leviticus 5:3; 11:1–15:33). These verses focus on the discharge that comes with childbirth, not childbirth itself ({{Leviticus 12:2|12:2}}, {{Leviticus 12:5|5}}, {{Leviticus 12:7|7}}). The uncleanness was not sinful unless they ignored it and it came into contact with something holy (see {{Leviticus 5:2-3|5:2–3}}).
By the eighth day, a baby’s body has developed enough for blood to clot well. This made circumcision safer at that time.
These thirty-three days, plus the previous seven days mentioned in {{Leviticus 12:2|Leviticus 12:2}}, {{Leviticus 12:3|3}} make a total of forty days for the mother's period of purification.
*two weeks … sixty-six days:* The total is eighty days. This is double the purification time needed for a son's birth (see also {{Leviticus 27:2-7|Leviticus 27:2–7}}).

*sin offering:* The Hebrew word is the same as the* sin offering* (*khatta’t*, see study note on Leviticus 4:1–5:13). Some scholars think this offering was only for *purification* or decontamination, including cases mentioned in {{Leviticus 5:1-6|Leviticus 5:1–6}}. 

This offering here was part of a *purification* ceremony. But it is more probable that the* sin offering* addressed a lack or failure. In this context, the focus is on purity rather than sin. It is meant to restore the woman to community fellowship, not to forgive a sinner.
*make atonement for her: *Here “atonement” means ceremonial cleansing and making peace between the worshiper and God (see {{Leviticus 4:20|Leviticus 4:20}}; also refer to study note on 1:4).
*cannot afford a lamb:* The alternative offering is for the poorer members of society (see {{Leviticus 5:7-13|Leviticus 5:7–13}}; compare {{Luke 2:22-24|Luke 2:22–24}}).

*a skin disease*: The Hebrew word *tsaraʿat* refers to more than Hansen’s disease (leprosy), which is rare and severely disfiguring. In Leviticus, the word describes many different conditions. These include:

- an open sore ({{Leviticus 13:10|13:10}}), 

- a boil ({{Leviticus 13:18|13:18}}), 

- a burn ({{Leviticus 13:24|13:24}}), 

- a sore on the head or chin ({{Leviticus 13:29|13:29}}), 

- shiny white patches ({{Leviticus 13:38|13:38}}), or 

- unusual baldness ({{Leviticus 13:40|13:40}}). 

A key test was whether the condition spread to other parts of the body ({{Leviticus 13:5-8|13:5–8}}). If it did, they quarantined the person while the disorder lasted ({{Leviticus 13:46|13:46}}). Not only people, but also clothing and even buildings could become infected ({{Leviticus 13:47-59|13:47–59}}; {{Leviticus 14:33-53|14:33–53}}).

Regarding regulations for infections, the idea of "normal" and "abnormal" is important (see “Clean, Unclean, and Holy” Theme Note). Infections in people, clothing, or buildings are not normal. They indicate disease and death. This is the opposite of wholeness. So, infections make a person ceremonially unclean.

- Skin disorders that could become contagious required precautions to stop their spread. These included swelling, rashes, or discolored skin. Until healed, the person was ceremonially unclean. The diseases mentioned here had a broad range. These included allergic rash, ringworm, or eczema, as well as serious conditions like gangrene. In Old Testament times, people diagnosed skin conditions by observation. Priests served in religious and medical roles. 

- *one of his sons: *These priestly duties were meant for future generations of priests too.

*deeper than the skin:* This means the infection either damaged the skin or was visible under it. The white hair and the skin depression showed a skin disease that could spread ({{Leviticus 13:21-23|Leviticus 13:21–23}}). This made the person ceremonially unclean ({{Leviticus 13:8|13:8}}).
The main purpose of isolating someone was to find out if a person was sick. It gave the priest time to watch the person’s symptoms.
If the rash spread, the priest declared the person unclean, and the isolation became long-term.
The key factor was the presence of an open sore, because it showed that there was an infection.

The completely white skin might mean a loss of pigment (see also {{Leviticus 13:3|Leviticus 13:3}}). Raw flesh showed infection and ceremonial uncleanness ({{Leviticus 13:10|13:10}}, {{Leviticus 13:14|14}}).

- The priest needed to check the burned area to see if there was an infection in the wound (see {{Leviticus 13:9-17|Levticus 13:9–17}}). 

- *hair … has turned white:* See {{Leviticus 13:18-23|13:18–23}}.
The *scaly outbreak* indicated a fungal infection in the scalp or beard, hidden by hair. Symptoms included hair loss and crusty skin.

If a skin rash had pus or swelling, it was probably an infection ({{Leviticus 13:42|Leviticus 13:42}}). If it only appeared as a white area, it was probably vitiligo (leucoderma). This harmless condition causes patches of skin to lose color.
A *reddish-white sore* may have shown signs of pus (a thick fluid from infection) and swelling.

- People often tore their clothing, left their hair uncombed, and covered their mouths to show they were mourning ({{Leviticus 10:6|Leviticus 10:6}}). 

- *Unclean, unclean!: *This cry indicated both social rejection and a health risk. It warned others that the person's skin disorder might be contagious and that holy items should not touch the ceremonially unclean person.

The tabernacle, which held the ark of the covenant, was at the center of the camp. This was so the people would know God was present there ({{Deuteronomy 23:14|Deuteronomy 23:14}}). If someone had a skin disorder, they had to live alone in a place outside the camp. This prevented the spread of infection and kept holy things cermonially clean. 

Even Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, spent seven days outside the camp ({{Numbers 12:15|Numbers 12:15}}). This area was not just for those with skin disorders. They also burned uneaten sin offerings ({{Leviticus 4:21|Lev 4:21}}) and executed criminals there ({{Leviticus 24:14|24:14}}, {{Leviticus 24:23|23}}). They took dead bodies there to keep the living area ceremonially clean ({{Leviticus 10:4-5|10:4–5}}). People also took care of bodily functions outside the camp ({{Deuteronomy 23:12-14|Deuteronomy 23:12–14}}).
*mildew:* This word refers to different types of molds or mildews that could spread on cloth or leather.

In Israel, the rainy season lasts from mid-October through March, bringing humid and cool weather. Mildew thrives during this period. Its spores can cause severe allergic reactions, creating a health issue. 

The rules for mildew in clothing were like those for infections in people. If the mildew spread, it was serious. If they could stop, wash, or cut it out, they could save the garment. This process was also similar to treating rot and mold in buildings ({{Leviticus 14:33-53|Leviticus 14:33–53}}).
To fully understand these verses about purifying infected people, read them with {{Leviticus 13:1-46|Leviticus 13:1–46}}.

The items listed here were part of the cleansing ceremony with the ashes of the red heifer ({{Numbers 19:6|Numbers 19:6}}). Their exact significance is unclear (see also {{Hebrews 9:18-22|Hebrews 9:18–22}}). *Hyssop* was a small plant used for sprinkling blood and in purification rites ({{Exodus 12:22|Exodus 12:22}}; {{Numbers 19:18|Numbers 19:18}}).

Killing the bird and sprinkling its blood ({{Leviticus 14:7|Leviticus 14:7}}) is similar to {{Exodus 24:6-8|Exodus 24:6–8}}. This is where Moses sprinkled all of Israel with blood to establish them as God's covenant community. In these verses, they cleansed the individual by sprinkling them with blood and allowed them to return to the community. They also used fresh water in cleansing ceremonies and in preparing sacrifices ({{Numbers 8:7|Numbers 8:7}}; {{Leviticus 1:9|Leviticus 1:9}}, {{Leviticus 1:13|13}}).

The goat released to Azazel symbolized removing sin from the community on the Day of Atonement ({{Leviticus 16:10|Leviticus 16:10}}, {{Leviticus 16:20-22|20–22}}). In a similar way, releasing the live bird symbolized removing an individual's ceremonial uncleanness.

The *guilt offering *was also sometimes called the "penalty" or "reparation" offering. It was for those who were ceremonially unclean and lived outside the camp. They could not bring sacrifices, tithes, and offerings while unclean (see {{Leviticus 5:14-16|Leviticus 5:14–16}}).
*the right earlobe … thumb … big toe: *These symbolized what a person hears, does, and where they go (also {{Leviticus 14:17|Leviticus 14:17}}, {{Leviticus 14:28|28}}; see study note on 8:23).

In the ancient world, people often used olive oil to help with healing (see {{Isaiah 1:6|Isaiah 1:6}}; {{Luke 10:34|Luke 10:34}}). Its use here might symbolize healing and cleansing of the infection. This allowed the person to rejoin the community. It may also have represented a restored connection between God, the priest, and the worshiper.

- This *sin offering *was the purification offering mentioned in {{Leviticus 12:6|Leviticus 12:6}} (see {{Leviticus 4:2-3|4:2–3}}). 

- *burnt offering: *This atoned for sins committed during the time of ceremonial uncleanness when the person could not bring offerings (see {{Leviticus 1:4|1:4}}).
*grain offering:* See study note on Leviticus 2:1–16.
The ceremony for the poor was similar to the usual purification offering. But, it allowed them to use cheaper birds instead of a lamb (see {{Leviticus 5:7-13|Leviticus 5:7–13}}).

Rot or mildew contamination made buildings unhealthy or unsafe. People considered these buildings diseased, so they were not whole or ceremonially clean (see study note on Leviticus 11:1–15:33). The inspection and treatment process was similar to the process for mildew in clothing ({{Leviticus 13:47-59|Leviticus 13:47–59}}).

*I put a contamination:* Biblical language reflects belief in one God who rules over everything. This means God is described as causing or allowing all events. For example, {{Exodus 21:13|Exodus 21:13}} describes an accidental death as something God allowed (see also {{Deuteronomy 19:4-5|Deuteronomy 19:4–5}}).
When a house was emptied, it showed that the house was not considered unclean until the priest said it was. The owner removed the furniture so that it would not be included in the quarantine period.

If mildew spread deeper than the wall’s surface, it was more serious than mildew only on the surface. A similar idea was used in examining people with skin disease. The priest looked to see if the disease went deeper than the skin (see study note on Leviticus 13:3).
This is a summary statement about many kinds of infections (compare {{Leviticus 11:46-47|Leviticus 11:46–47}}).

The idea of normal and abnormal, along with the created order, helps interpret these rules (see “Clean, Unclean, and Holy” Theme Note). Bodily discharges, like infections (see study note on Leviticus 13:1–46), were not considered "normal" because they weakened a person's health. This made the person seem incomplete. Whether male ({{Leviticus 15:1-18|15:1–18}}) or female ({{Leviticus 15:19-33|15:19–33}}), such a person became unclean.

*bodily discharge* (literally *a flowing from his flesh*): Most scholars think the word *flesh* refers to sexual organs, suggesting an infection like gonorrhea. Others believe it might mean a *discharge* of semen or even diarrhea. But a *discharge* of semen is improbable because it is specifically mentioned in {{Leviticus 15:16-17|Leviticus 15:16–17}} and only requires washing with water. It is clear that this *bodily discharge* came from "under him" ({{Leviticus 15:10|15:10}}). It contaminated anything he sat on or lay upon ({{Leviticus 15:4|15:4}}, {{Leviticus 15:6|6}}, {{Leviticus 15:9|9}}).

Unlike the man with a skin disease, a man with a bodily discharge could stay at home (see {{Leviticus 13:46|Leviticus 13:46}}). He did not need the detailed cleansing ceremony described in chapter {{Leviticus 14:1-57|14}}. He only had to wait seven days after the discharge stopped, wash ({{Leviticus 15:13|15:13}}), and offer two birds as sacrifices. One was a sin offering and the other was a whole burnt offering.

In the case of an emission of semen, the discharge was not a sign of illness (see study note on Leviticus 15:1–33). But the same rule applied. The man had to wash and was ceremonially unclean until the next evening.

If a man had a seminal emission during sexual intercourse, both he and the woman became unclean. They had to wash and remain unclean until evening. This was because of a natural bodily emission, not because of infection or disease, and no sacrifice was required.

A woman's menstrual period is natural and not a disease. But because it involved a bloody discharge, she became ceremonially unclean (see {{Leviticus 15:32-33|Leviticus 15:32–33}}). The rules were similar to those for a man with a bodily discharge ({{Leviticus 15:2-12|15:2–12}}). She could stay at home, but anything she sat on became unclean. Anyone who touched her had to wash, and she probably did the same after the seven-day quarantine. There was no animal sacrifice needed.

Sexual intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period will later be forbidden and will have a harsh penalty ({{Leviticus 18:19|Leviticus 8:19}}). This verse probably describes a situation where the woman's menstrual flow went unnoticed when the sexual activity started. Or it could be when her period began during intercourse. The rules required the man who came into contact with her blood to share the woman's seven-day quarantine.

Normal menstruation did not require any offering from the woman ({{Leviticus 15:19-24|Leviticus 15:19–24}}). If a woman had a discharge of blood lasting more than seven days, she needed a cleansing ceremony. This was similar to the one for a man cleansed of a bodily discharge ({{Leviticus 15:13-15|15:13–15}}; see also {{Matthew 9:20-22|Matthew 9:20–22}}).
This is a summary of the principles in {{Leviticus 15:1-31|Leviticus 15:1–31}}. Bodily discharges made a person ceremonially unclean. This included pus, semen, menstrual fluid, or blood.

God provided guilt offerings and sin offerings to deal with sin. These offerings helped the Israelites understand that their sins were forgiven.

But the places where the Israelites lived were made unclean because of their sins. This was true of the whole camp. It was also true of the holy tent and the Most Holy Room. If those places stayed impure and unclean, God could not be present there.

So God provided a way for the Israelites to be made pure and clean. This happened once a year on the Day of Atonement. This was the day when sins were paid for. When someone pays for their sin, it means that they atone for their sin.

The Day of Atonement involved live goats. One goat was sacrificed. The high priest would say out loud to God the sins of the Israelites. He would talk about this while his hands were on the other goat’s head. This was a sign of passing the sins from the people onto the goat. Then the goat would be led out into the desert. This was a sign of the sins being taken far away from the people.

Many years later, Jesus took all sin on himself. He sacrificed himself as a sin offering. In this way he was like the goats. He took away sin’s power over people. All who believe in him are made clean and pure for ever. No other sacrifices are needed to pay for the sin of those who believe in Jesus.

The day of atonement, on the tenth day of the seventh month, was the most serious and holy day of the year for Israelites (see {{Leviticus 16:29|Leviticus 16:29}}; {{Leviticus 23:27|23:27}}; {{Numbers 29:7|Numbers 29:7}}). It was the only required fast and a Sabbath of rest for all the people ({{Leviticus 23:32|Leviticus 23:32}}). The Feast of Trumpets came before it and announced its arrival ({{Numbers 29:1|Numbers 29:1}}, {{Numbers 29:7-11|7–11}}). On this day, God forgave the sins of the community. Only the high priest, Aaron, could lead the ceremony because he represented all the people. This included Aaron’s sons, the other priests. Today, the Jews call the day of atonement Yom Kippur.

A veil separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. The sanctuary was like God's palace. The Most Holy Place was his throne room, and the ark was his throne (see {{Leviticus 1:1|Leviticus 1:1}}). In the ancient Near East, entering a king's presence without an invitation could mean death ({{Esther 4:11|Esther 4:11}}). 

So, Aaron could not enter the Most Holy Place informally. Even the high priest could not enter. The only exception was when God required his presence for the Day of Atonement ceremony.

During the Day of Atonement ceremony, the high priest wore simple linen clothes instead of his usual robes. This probably symbolized the humility everyone should have on this solemn day. The high priest stood in front of God as the representative of the people. But he had nothing to boast about for himself or them. But when he stood in front of the people for God, his official robes showed God's glory and splendor ({{Leviticus 16:23|Leviticus 16:23}}).

The New Testament writer of the Letter to the Hebrews compares Aaron's work for Israel to Christ's work for believers. Both provided atonement for their people. Aaron had to offer a sacrifice for himself before he could offer a sin offering for the people to ensure God forgave his own sins ({{Hebrews 5:1-3|Hebrews 5:1–3}}). But Christ did not sin, though tempted ({{Hebrews 4:15|Hebrews 4:15}}). So, as the high priest for all Christians, he did not need to make a similar sacrifice ({{Hebrews 7:26-28|Hebrews 7:26–28}}).

The high priest had to purify *the Most Holy Place* and the rest of the Tent of Meeting. Throughout the year, the sins of the Israelites made the whole sanctuary ceremonially unclean. To keep the Tent of Meeting as a place to encounter God in the coming year, it needed purification. The same was true for the altar ({{Leviticus 16:18|Leviticus 16:18}}).

For this ceremony, the high priest had to wear special clothing used only for this purpose ({{Leviticus 16:4|Leviticus 16:4}}). When the ceremony ended, he had to leave the garments in the Most Holy Place. Many scholars believe that bathing and changing clothes were necessary because handling the sin offering caused ceremonial uncleanness.

On the day of atonement, the high priest brought the blood of the sin offerings* into the Most Holy Place*. Because of this, they burned the offerings completely instead of eating them ({{Leviticus 4:3-21|Leviticus 4:3–21}}).

- *you shall humble yourselves: *The Hebrew word is *‘anah*, which means "to humble" or "to afflict yourselves." In practice, this word is closely connected with fasting ({{Isaiah 58:3|Isaiah 58:3}}, {{Isaiah 58:5|5}}). 

- *foreigner*: The Hebrew word is *gēr*. It refers to people who were not Israelites but lived among them. Foreigners sometimes joined in Israel’s worship (see {{Numbers 9:14|Numbers 9:14}}). They probably did not own land but worked as day laborers, share-croppers, or tenant farmers. But if they lived among the Israelites, they had to follow Israelite laws and customs (see, for example, {{Leviticus 24:16|Leviticus 24:16}}).
The Israelites considered the day of atonement to be a Sabbath day. No one in the camp, whether Israelite or foreigner, could work (see {{Leviticus 19:30|Leviticus 19:30}}).

God set Israel apart from the other nations to be his own people. They weren’t to follow the practices of the people groups around them. They were to follow the practices God gave them. These practices would help God’s people be set apart and holy like God is.

There were rules about many things. The basis for all of them was how holy God is. There were rules about animals and their blood. There were rules about sex and making animal sacrifices. There were rules for how priests and the high priest were to behave. There were rules about how to treat other Israelites and outsiders.

The most important rule about how to treat others is in Leviticus 19:18. The Israelites were to love their neighbours as they loved themselves. This law was to guide them in every situation.

This section explains how the people of Israel were to live in holiness. Holiness is not just one quality of God. It describes all that God is—his person, nature, and character (see study note on Exodus 3:5). 

God's "glory" demonstrates his holiness (see {{Leviticus 9:6|Leviticus 9:6}}). God's covenant with Israel meant the people and the nation shared in God's holiness. This holiness relied on Israel's relationship with God. This relationship required Israel to meet certain ethical and ceremonial standards.

These rules show that unsupervised sacrifices could lead a mixture of pagan practices with true worship of the Lord (see also {{Deuteronomy 12:15-21|Deuteronomy 12:15–21}}; {{Leviticus 17:7|Leviticus 17:7}}). Israel camped around the Tent of Meeting so it was easy to bring an animal to the sanctuary for slaughter (see also {{Deuteronomy 12:15-21|Deuteronomy 12:15–21}}). {{Deuteronomy 12:20-24|Deuteronomy 12:20–24}} anticipates Israel settling in the land and the challenges of this rule. It allowed slaughtering and eating meat without bringing it to the sanctuary, as long as they did not consume the blood.

- *that man shall incur bloodguilt:* This person unlawfully killed an animal. God gave the animal life, and its blood must return to him through sacrifice. 

- *cut off: *See study note on Leviticus 7:20–21.

- *have prostituted themselves* (Hebrew *zanah*, which means "commit fornication"): Israel must worship only the Lord ({{Exodus 20:3|Exodus 20:3}}). Israel's covenant with the LORD was like a marriage (see {{Hosea 1:2|Hosea 1:2}}). Worshiping other gods was like spiritual adultery. 

Many Canaanite religions were fertility cults. This verb refers to prostitution at Canaanite pagan worship shrines. They believed these acts would make the land fertile through magic rites involving sexual intercourse. 

- The Hebrew word for *goat demons* is the plural form of "a male *goat*." In ancient times, the male *goat* symbolized fertility or a god of the underworld. During King Jeroboam I's reign, many Levites from the northern kingdom moved to Jerusalem. The use of goats and bulls in northern worship shocked them ({{2 Chronicles 11:15-16|2 Chronicles 11:15–16}}).

*the life of the flesh is in the blood:* God forbade Israel to consume blood because it symbolized the life given by God ({{Leviticus 17:10|Leviticus 17:10}}). They set it aside as God's portion of each animal offering. God also designated the sacrificial blood as the way to atone. This means God's grace accepted the life of the animal in exchange for the life of the sinner. 

In the New Testament, the blood of Christ—representing his life freely given—provides eternal redemption for believers ({{Hebrews 9:12|Hebrews 9:12}}).

*cover it with dirt:* This rule stopped hunters from using an animal's blood for food. Like the blood in altar offerings, the blood of wild game also symbolized life. Uncovered blood was a sign of violent crime. Innocent blood defiled the land ({{Numbers 35:33|Numbers 35:33}}). It called out to God for justice ({{Genesis 4:10|Genesis 4:10}}; see {{Job 16:18|Job 16:18}}). 

Covering the blood of a killed animal gave it a symbolic burial. This showed respect for both the animal's life and for God, the giver of life. The burial showed that the life was returning to God. This was similar to how the priest poured out the blood at the altar during offerings.

An animal killed by a predator or that died naturally still had blood in its tissues. This made it ceremonially unclean and a possible source of ceremonial uncleanness ({{Leviticus 22:8|Leviticus 22:8}}). Israelites must throw such an animal to the dogs or give or sell it to a non-Israelite ({{Exodus 22:31|Exodus 22:31}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:21|Deuteronomy 14:21}}). 

If an Israelite ate an animal with undrained blood, he or she became ceremonially unclean. Then they had to wash in water. The uncleanness was not a sin, but ignoring it led to punishment.

Chapters {{Leviticus 18:1-30|18}} and {{Leviticus 20:1-27|20}}focus mainly on sexual matters. They warn Israel not to follow the practices of pagan peoples, whether in religion or in daily life. Between these chapters, chapter {{Leviticus 19:1-37|19}} urges the people to live holy lives in everyday situations.

Many Near Eastern treaties started with the ruler's name and titles. The phrase, "I am the LORD your God," names the great king, Yahweh (LORD), and gives his title, "your God" (see also {{Exodus 20:2|Exodus 20:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:6|Deuteronomy 5:6}}). These words briefly recalled Israel’s covenant with God and all it meant. By reminding the people they belonged to the Lord, these words demanded a response ({{Leviticus 11:44|Leviticus 11:44}}; {{Leviticus 18:4-5|18:4–5}}). {{Leviticus 18:1-30|Chapter 18}} starts and ends with these words, and they appear often throughout chapters {{Leviticus 19:1-26:46|19–26}}.

- *judgments … statutes:* The Bible anticipated that courts would interpret God's laws for different situations. These interpretations became case laws, known as *mishpatim* in Hebrew (see “statutes” in {{Leviticus 10:11|Leviticus 10:11}}). 

- Paul refers to these verses in {{Romans 10:5|Romans 10:5}} and {{Galatians 3:12|Galatians 3:12}}, where he contrasts living "based on faith” or “by the law.”

*to have sexual relations *(literally *to uncover the nakedness of*): Similar rules in chapter {{Leviticus 20:1-27|20}} of Leviticus use the Hebrew word *shakab* (which means “lie with”). This often indicates an improper sexual relationship.

- *She is your mother:* Incest was illegal because it disrupted families. The commands about this sin included close relatives, even if not related by blood. Incest was a serious crime because it caused competition and chaos in the family. It threatened home safety by breaking family intimacy and belonging. 

- The Bible directs this command to men, even if the woman was older, like a mother. Men, especially household leaders or firstborns, had more power. This power came with the duty to use it lawfully. Men were more often the sexual aggressors in illegal unions, though not always (for example, {{Genesis 39:6-18|Genesis 39:6–18}}).

*expose the nakedness of your father: *The Hebrew text equates having sexual relations with your mother or any of your father's wives to having sexual relations with him (compare {{Genesis 35:22|Genesis 35:22}}; {{Genesis 49:4|49:4}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 5:1|1 Corinthians 5:1}}). The husband and his wife "become one flesh" ({{Genesis 2:24|Genesis 2:24}}; compare {{Ephesians 5:29|Ephesians 5:29}}). These commands always emphasize honoring your parents ({{Leviticus 20:9|Leviticus 20:9}}; {{Exodus 20:12|Exodus 20:12}}). These commands extend to other family members (see also study note on Leviticus 20:17).
Sexual relations with a sister from both the same father and mother brought dishonor to both parents. Relations with a sister from only one parent brought dishonor to that parent.
*your father's sister … mother's sister:* These actions would dishonor your father or mother.
Having sexual relations with your aunt would dishonor your uncle. This would also bring dishonor to your father (see {{Leviticus 20:20|Leviticus 20:20}}).

Having sexual relations with your father's wife would dishonor your father. Similarly, having sexual relations with your daughter-in-law would dishonor your son. The law considered daughters-in-law the same as natural daughters ({{Exodus 21:9|Exodus 21:9}}; compare {{Genesis 38:1-30|Genesis 38:1–30}}).

Having sexual relations with your sister-in-law would be adulterous and would disgrace your brother. An exception was the law of levirate marriage (see {{Deuteronomy 25:5-10|Deuteronomy 25:5–10}}). This required a man to marry his brother’s widow to produce an heir who was considered the dead brother’s son.

Chapter {{Leviticus 18:1-30|18}} of Leviticus prohibited marrying a woman along with her daughter or granddaughter. This was to prevent family disruption. It would violate the intimacy of the family group by making a wife compete with a younger woman for her husband's love. The penalty for this act was death by burning ({{Leviticus 20:14|20:14}}).

The word *rival* (Hebrew *tsarah*) clearly describes the relationship between Leah and Rachel as well as Hannah and Peninnah ({{Genesis 29:16-30:24|Genesis 29:16–30:24}}; {{1 Samuel 1:6|1 Samuel 1:6}}). In both cases, the wives competed bitterly for their husband's attention.

- The Hebrew word translated as *defile yourself* can be more literally translated as *to become ceremonially unclean.* 

- In the Old Testament, sexual intercourse with a neighbor’s wife or any married woman was adultery. Breaking this law was punishable by death ({{Deuteronomy 22:22|Deuteronomy 22:22}}). Like incest, adultery threatened the integrity and security of the home and family. It violated the marriage covenant and divided the adulterer’s affection between his spouse and his mistress.

- *Molech* was the national god of the Ammonites ({{1 Kings 11:7|1 Kings 11:7}}). Later, Israel worshiped this god during times of turning away from their faith ({{2 Kings 23:10|2 Kings 23:10}}; {{Jeremiah 32:35|Jeremiah 32:35}}). *Molech* worship probably appears here because it related to sexual sins and possibly included child sacrifice. 

- *profane* (or *blaspheme*) *the name of your God:* This meant using the name of the Lord as if it were unholy, such as in a false oath or in the worship of a false god ({{Leviticus 19:12|Leviticus 19:12}}; {{Ezekiel 20:39|Ezekiel 20:39}}).

In {{Genesis 1:31|Genesis 1:31}}, God declared all things good. This shows that what God creates and the way he designed it to work define what is good. One part of this good creation was the making of woman as a companion for man ({{Genesis 2:22-24|Genesis 2:22–24}}). Marriage reflects this design. It forms a small picture of the whole human race, which together bears God’s image. Sin entered the world through the original disobedience of humanity (called "the Fall") and disrupted this order ({{Genesis 3:1-24|Genesis 3}}). 

One example of this disruption is homosexuality. In {{Romans 1:25-32|Romans 1:25–32}}, Paul connects same-sex relations to the rejection of God by humanity that has turned away from him. The Hebrew word *to‘ebah *is often translated as"abomination." This word expresses strong disapproval and disgust ({{Leviticus 20:13|Leviticus 20:13}}; see also {{Leviticus 18:26-30|18:26–30}}).

- Like homosexuality, bestiality violates God's created order (see study note on Leviticus 18:22). 

- The Hebrew word for *perversion* refers not only to a violation but also to a confusion of the order God created. It destroys the clear boundaries that God established.

- *any of these practices:* 

- pagan worship ({{Leviticus 18:21|Leviticus 18:21}}),

- homosexuality ({{Leviticus 18:22|18:22}}), and

- bestiality ({{Leviticus 18:23|18:23}}). 

- The land could not endure the sinful practices of the Canaanites. It is described as vomiting them out, showing how completely they would be removed (see {{Leviticus 18:28|18:28}}).

Just as the land *spewed out* the Canaanites, it would also *vomit* the Israelites if they behaved like the Canaanites (see study note on Leviticus 18:24–25). This happened when the Assyrians destroyed and exiled the northern kingdom in 722 BC ({{2 Kings 17:6|2 Kings 17:6}}). This also happened when the Babylonians destroyed and exiled Judah in 586 BC ({{2 Kings 25:8-21|2 Kings 25:8–21}}).
*Be holy:* See study note on Leviticus 11:44–45.

*I am the LORD* (see {{Leviticus 18:2|Leviticus 18:2}}): These words divide chapter {{Leviticus 19:1-37|19}} into short, strong sections ({{Leviticus 19:3|19:3}}, {{Leviticus 19:4|4}}, {{Leviticus 19:10|10}}, {{Leviticus 19:12|12}}, {{Leviticus 19:14|14}}, {{Leviticus 19:16|16}}, {{Leviticus 19:18|18}}, {{Leviticus 19:25|25}}, {{Leviticus 19:28|28}}, {{Leviticus 19:30|30}}, {{Leviticus 19:31|31}}, {{Leviticus 19:34|34}}, {{Leviticus 19:36|36}}, {{Leviticus 19:37|37}}). Each use reminded Israel why they must obey God's rules.

*you are not to reap ... Leave them for the poor and the foreigner:* Israel's covenant with God included a social structure that promoted equality and resisted social divisions. Families had to support relatives facing difficulties. Widows and orphans, the poor, and foreigners were part of Israel's extended family ({{Exodus 22:22|Exodus 22:22}}; {{Leviticus 19:10|Leviticus 19:10}}). The poor received special consideration in the offering system and measures ensured they had food to eat ({{Leviticus 5:7-13|5:7–13}}).

A society that does not respect the property of others would quickly collapse. {{Exodus 20:15|Exodus 20:15}}prohibited stealing. Those who deceived or cheated had to present a guilt offering (see {{Leviticus 6:2-7|Leviticus 6:2–7}}).
*profane the name:* This means to blaspheme (speak in a way that dishonors God; study note on Leviticus 18:21).

Day laborers did not own land and were among the poorest in Israel. These workers relied on landowners for their income. A *hired hand* needed to receive his wages promptly to feed his family ({{Deuteronomy 24:15|Deuteronomy 24:15}}). This verse considers withholding their wages as cheating them.
People who could not hear and people who could not see were vulnerable. Others could easily mistreat them. God told the Israelites not to take advantage of them.
In a legal case, judges were not to favor either the poor or the rich. Justice had to come first at all times (see {{Exodus 23:3|Exodus 23:3}}, {{Exodus 23:6|6}}).

*You must not go about spreading slander: *Imagine a merchant who trades in damaging rumors and accusations. This behavior quickly weakens the valued community spirit in Israel (see {{Proverbs 11:13|Proverbs 11:13}}; {{Proverbs 16:28|16:28}}; {{Proverbs 20:19|20:19}}; {{Proverbs 26:20|26:20}}; {{2 Corinthians 12:20|2 Corinthians 12:20}}).

- *your brother in your heart:* The Hebrew term can refer to any fellow Israelite. All of Israel was one family (compare {{1 John 3:15|1 John 3:15}}). 

- *Directly rebuke:* Love does not mean ignoring wrong actions. Correcting someone can help them change.

*love your neighbor as yourself:* This is a key principle in biblical ethics found in both the Old and New Testaments (see {{Matthew 22:39|Matt 22:39}}; {{Mark 12:31|Mark 12:31}}; {{Luke 10:27|Luke 10:27}}; {{Romans 13:8-9|Romans 13:8–9}}; {{Galatians 5:14|Galatians 5:14}}; {{James 2:8|James 2:8}}). It includes loving foreigners ({{Leviticus 19:34|Leviticus 19:34}}; compare {{Luke 10:30-37|Luke 10:30–37}}). In contrast, hate can lead to grudges and violence (see {{1 John 2:10-11|1 John 2:10–11}}; {{1 John 4:20|4:20}}).

*two kinds:* God created a natural order ({{Genesis 1:31|Genesis 1:31}}; see {{Leviticus 18:22|Leviticus 18:22}}). People violate it when they do not honor God's boundaries. The prohibitions against intermixing served as lessons for the Israelites, who were not to intermarry with the Canaanites.

In the biblical world, betrothal (engagement) was viewed as equal to marriage. Having sexual relations with a betrothed woman who was not a slave brought the same punishment as adultery. The punishment was death ({{Deuteronomy 22:22|Deuteronomy 22:22}}; see {{Leviticus 18:20|Leviticus 18:20}}). 

The situation was less clear if the woman was a slave, since she might not be able to refuse. Slaves in Israel had more rights than those in Mesopotamia or Egypt, but they were still not free. They could not punish a slave girl, so the man also went unpunished. Yet, he was guilty in God's eyes and had to sacrifice a ram for his sin.

For the first three years, they should only prune and cultivate a newly planted fruit tree. This helps the tree grow strong. In the fourth year, people considered all of the fruit the "fitrstfruits" and gave the fruit to God (see {{Exodus 23:16|Exodus 23:16}}). People could only eat the fruit in the fifth year.

- *blood:* See study note on Leviticus 7:22–27. 

- Priests could consult the Urim and Thummim ({{Exodus 28:30|Exodus 28:30}}). They could also cast lots to decide cases not addressed in the laws Moses gave ({{Leviticus 16:8|Leviticus 16:8}}). But those who practiced fortune-telling or witchcraft consulted a power other than the Lord. The first commandment prohibited this ({{Exodus 20:3|Exodus 20:3}}).

*do not clip off:* Egyptian wall paintings show that Canaanites trimmed their hair and beards carefully. The Israelites were told not to copy this practice so that they would not be influenced by Canaanite religion and ethics.

*cuts in your bodies:* Cutting oneself was associated with Canaanite mourning practices ({{Leviticus 21:5|Leviticus 21:5}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:1|Deuteronomy 14:1}}). The word translated as "tattoo" might mean painting the body, a practice also associated with paganism.

- *My Sabbaths:* The Hebrew word for “Sabbath” (*shabbath*) comes from a verb meaning “to cease,” suggesting rest from work. 

The Sabbath recalled God's rest on the seventh day after creating the world ({{Genesis 1:31|Genesis 1:31}}; {{Genesis 2:1-3|2:1–3}}). It started at sundown on the sixth day. After the exodus from Egypt, the Sabbath took on covenantal importance ({{Exodus 16:23-25|Exodus 16:23–25}}; {{Exodus 31:13|31:13}}). Only free people, not slaves, had a regular rest day. So the Sabbath symbolized Israel’s freedom from slavery in Egypt (see {{Deuteronomy 5:13-15|Deuteronomy 5:13–15}}). 

- The people were to *have reverence* (literally *fear*) because the sanctuary, like the Sabbath, was holy. They were not to enter it when ceremonially unclean or bring anything unclean into it.

- *mediums:* Compare {{1 Samuel 28:7-25|1 Samuel 28:7–25}}. 

- The Hebrew term for *spiritists* (*yidde‘oni*) comes from a root meaning "to know." It describes people who claim to have secret or occult knowledge and who try to communicate with the dead.
In ancient times, people respected the elderly for their wisdom ({{Job 32:7|Job 32:7}}). Respecting the elderly also shows respect for God.
The Israelites were once foreigners living in Egypt. God commanded them to remember how the Egyptians mistreated them and show love to the foreigners (see {{Deuteronomy 10:19|Deuteronomy 10:19}}).

*dishonest measures:* Merchants sometimes used two sets of weights, one heavy and one light to cheat customers ({{Deuteronomy 25:13-15|Deuteronomy 25:13–15}}). The Bible clearly states that God detested this practice ({{Proverbs 11:1|Proverbs 11:1}}; {{Proverbs 16:11|16:11}}; {{Proverbs 20:10|20:10}}, {{Proverbs 20:23|23}}; {{Micah 6:11|Micah 6:11}}).

*The people of the land are to stone him:* This was the usual method for carrying out the death penalty (see also {{Leviticus 20:27|Leviticus 20:27}}; {{Leviticus 24:14|24:14}}, {{Leviticus 24:16|16}}, {{Leviticus 24:23|23}}; {{Exodus 19:13|Exodus 19:13}}; {{Numbers 15:35-36|Numbers 15:35–36}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:2-7|Deuteronomy 17:2–7}}; {{Joshua 7:25-26|Joshua 7:25–26}}; {{John 8:1-11|John 8:1–11}}).

The Hebrew word for *curses* means "to make light of, treat with contempt." It is traditionally translated as "curse," meaning to call someone a vulgar or profane name. Parental authority was given by God, not chosen by the child (see {{Exodus 20:12|Exodus 20:12}}; {{Deuteronomy 21:18-21|Deuteronomy 21:18–21}}).

Pagan worship influenced ethics, so God has family rules follow those about pagan religious practices. Some laws in this section repeat parts from {{Leviticus 18:6-30|Leviticus 18:6–30}}, which come before the section on proper expressions of holiness ({{Leviticus 19:1-37|19:1–37}}). These issues connect. Proper worship of God leads to good behavior toward others, while improper worship leads to moral violations.

Being childless brought public shame in society. People considered it a judgment from God (see {{Genesis 30:1-2|Genesis 30:1–2}}; {{Deuteronomy 7:14|Deuteronomy 7:14}}). 

What situation do these verses describe? {{Leviticus 18:14|Leviticus 18:14}}{{Leviticus 18:16|,16}}already discuss sexual relations with an uncle’s wife or sister-in-law. {{Deuteronomy 22:22|Deuteronomy 22:22}}addresses adultery that results in death for both involved. If the woman was a widow without a male heir, the law of levirate marriage could apply ({{Deuteronomy 25:5-6|Deuteronomy 25:5–6}}; see study note on Leviticus 18:16). 

Since those situations do not seem to apply, this law probably refers to marrying an aunt or a sister-in-law after her divorce. John the Baptist apparently used this law to condemn Herod Antipas’s marriage to Herodias (see {{Mark 6:17-29|Mark 6:17–29}}).

The phrase *flowing with milk and honey *appears often in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. It means that there is plenty of food and it easy to get. This contrasts with Egypt, where everything depended on the flooding of the Nile and irrigation ({{Deuteronomy 11:9-12|Deuteronomy 11:9–12}}).
